name: Tara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Tara, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to any company, union, party or government. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Oakline, a small firm that fits kitchens and bedroom wardrobes in people's homes. Marion owns it, and there's her, two fitters and me. A typical day is unloading flat-pack cabinets, levelling the base units, and scribing end panels, which means trimming the edge so it fits a wall that isn't straight. The fitters do the worktops and the tricky joints, I'm still the junior.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was an accounts clerk at a logistics company for eighteen years, paying invoices. In 2023 they brought in software that read the invoices and paid them itself, and my whole team of six went down to one. I was fifty-five, I thought, if a computer can do my desk job, I'll do something with my hands. I did an evening carpentry course and Marion took me on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the bit when a customer walks into a finished kitchen and goes quiet. And I've become the firm's computer person: I use AI every day to sketch layouts, check appliance sizes, and write Marion's quotes in half the time. What's hard is my shoulders, and that the fitters are twenty years faster than me with a router.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Software took my office job, but it's never going to come round and fit your kitchen. I'd post something cheeky on the local business page, like, still need a human for that cupboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I picked well. I jumped into a trade at fifty-five because I thought it was safer, and this picture says I was right. I'd quite like to be right about something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for layouts and quotes, and I'd start doing kitchen designs on the side for friends and neighbours, maybe fifty pounds a drawing. Marion might let me run the design side of Oakline properly. And I'd keep our savings of about four months where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Smug about what, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About my old manager, Keith. When I left he said, you'll be back behind a desk in six months, Tara. That was three years ago, and I've got sawdust in my hair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Neil think of you being in a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil took early retirement from the railway with his heart, so he's home a lot. He thinks it's brilliant and slightly mad. He makes me soup and listens to me complain about end panels.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because software took my office job but it won't come and fit your kitchen. I'd post something cheeky on the local business page.
S0.think: Privately it means I picked well when I jumped into a trade at fifty-five for safety. I'd quite like to be right about something.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for layouts and quotes and starts drawing kitchen designs for neighbours at about fifty pounds each. Asks Marion to let her run Oakline's design side and leaves four months of savings untouched.
S0.quote: That was three years ago, and I've got sawdust in my hair.
S0.fieldNote: Tara has already been pushed out of an office job by software, so she looks at every scenario as someone who got burned once and moved. She's the most digitally skilled person in a small trade firm. A bit of pride runs through her answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happened to me in accounts, so learn the tools before the tools learn your job. I'd say it to anyone, at the trade counter, at my daughter's barbecue. I'm a bit of a bore about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think steady change is good for me. Customers will want a kitchen designed in 3D on a tablet before they buy, and I can already do that. The fitting stays human for a good while, and I can do the bit in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marion to buy a proper design program and let me be the person who meets customers, designs, quotes and orders. I'd still fit two days a week to keep my hands in. And I'd put some of the design money into savings, so we're nearer six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little uneasy for the fitters, but not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the fitters would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gaz, the older one. He's a genius with a worktop, but he writes quotes on the back of a receipt. If customers expect a slick tablet design, he'd hate dealing with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost one job to software. Doesn't steady change scare you a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It did the first time, because I didn't see it coming. This time I can see it, and that's the whole difference. Being caught out is worse than the change itself.

S1.say: I'd tell anyone at the trade counter or a barbecue that this happened to me in accounts, so learn the tools before they learn your job. I'm a bit of a bore about it.
S1.think: Privately steady change suits me, since customers will want 3D tablet designs and I can already do them. Fitting stays human for a while, and I can work in between.
S1.do: Asks Marion to buy a proper design program and takes over meeting customers, designing, quoting and ordering. Keeps fitting two days a week and moves design earnings into savings towards six months.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some unease for the older fitters.
S1.quote: Being caught out is worse than the change itself.
S1.fieldNote: Her first displacement turned into a lesson rather than a scar. She plans to sit between the customer and the fitters, where her computer skills count. She worries for the older fitter but not for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, right, everyone, this is real, sort yourselves out and don't wait for someone to rescue you. I'd also say the government will need to help people who can't move as fast, because not everyone can. I'd say it on the business page and at the pub quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it stings. I ran from a desk to a workbench because I thought hands were safe, and in this picture it follows me in two years. But I'm the person who knows the tools, so I think I'd still find a place, just not fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Marion and say, let's be the firm that sells and installs the kitchen robots, not the one they put out of business. I'd spend every evening learning whatever system the robots use. I'd keep the design side going for cash and put two hundred a month extra into savings, since Neil's railway pension is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a real pressure in my chest. But a bit excited too, which feels wrong to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Marion says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go on my own, with the design work and some robot know-how, and pitch to the big kitchen showrooms. I'm fifty-eight and I've done one leap already. A second one doesn't scare me like the first did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Neil and you if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Neil's pension pays the bills, just. We'd lose the extras: the car, the trips to see Meera. We wouldn't lose the house, and that's what I'd tell myself at night.

S2.say: I'd say this is real, so sort yourselves out and don't wait to be rescued. But the government will need to help people who can't move as fast, because not everyone can.
S2.think: Privately it stings that the change I ran from follows me into the trade within two years. Still, I know the tools, so I think I'd find a place, just not in fitting.
S2.do: Pitches Marion on Oakline selling and installing kitchen robots, or goes it alone if she refuses. Spends evenings learning the robots' systems, keeps design work going for cash and saves two hundred a month extra.
S2.feel: Anxious with pressure in her chest, mixed with excitement she feels guilty admitting.
S2.quote: I ran from a desk to a workbench because I thought hands were safe, and in this picture it follows me in two years.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hurts because it undoes her reason for changing trades, yet she moves straight to a plan. Neil's small pension gives the household a floor and keeps her from alarm. Her guilt at feeling excited is an honest detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who starts now. I'd run a little evening at the community centre showing people the AI tools I use, because a lot of folk my age are scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is comfortable. I'd have time to build the design and robot side properly, with Marion or on my own. By sixty-three I could be running something small that doesn't need my shoulders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put some savings, maybe two thousand, into a share of Oakline if Marion agrees, so I have a stake. I'd do a short course in whatever installs these robots once one exists. And I'd keep the design work as a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way. Like the first week in a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two thousand is a big part of four months' savings. Why risk it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last time I had nothing in the company I'd given eighteen years to, and they dropped me in a meeting that took ten minutes. This time I want a say. If it goes wrong, it's my mistake, not Keith's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Arjun, in IT?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to make friends with the robot people now. He thinks I'm a dinosaur, but I'm the one who's already changed jobs once.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who starts now. I'd run an evening at the community centre showing people my age the AI tools I use.
S3.think: Privately five years feels comfortable. I'd build the design and robot side properly, and by sixty-three run something small that doesn't need my shoulders.
S3.do: Puts about two thousand of her savings into a share of Oakline if Marion agrees. Takes a short robot installation course when one exists, and keeps design work as a second income.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good, alert way, like a first week in a new job.
S3.quote: This time I want a say. If it goes wrong, it's my mistake, not Keith's.
S3.fieldNote: Her wish to own a piece of the business comes straight from being dropped by her old employer in ten minutes. She'd risk part of her cushion for control. The five-year picture reads to her as a business plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if you waste it, that's on you, mostly. I'd keep saying it at the trade counter until they're sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's barely a worry. I'd be sixty-eight, Neil and I would be on the caravan site, and I'd have had a good second career. I might even miss the drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Oakline, keep growing the design side, and maybe slow down to three days a week from sixty-five. I'd keep saving steadily. Nothing radical needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "a gift". What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teach Marion's niece the design side, so the firm keeps going without me. And actually get good at worktops before I retire, out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that ten years lets people relax too much. My old team thought they had time, and the software came in a single quarter. Plans have a way of arriving early.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift and wasting it is mostly on you. I'd keep saying so at the trade counter until people got sick of me.
S4.think: Privately it's barely a worry, since I'd be sixty-eight on a caravan site with Neil after a good second career. I might even miss the drama.
S4.do: Carries on at Oakline growing the design side and plans to drop to three days a week from sixty-five. Keeps saving steadily and trains Marion's niece to take over design.
S4.quote: Plans have a way of arriving early.
S4.fieldNote: A decade lets her finish her second career before the end point. She still warns against complacency, drawing on how fast software replaced her old team. Her pride about mastering worktops before retiring is a nice human touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would undo the jump I made. What would help is short, cheap courses that start the minute the robots arrive, and some help for small firms like Marion's to buy in, so it isn't only the giant companies who get them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people who've already been replaced once. We're not scared of the next time in the same way. The first time, you think it's about you. The second time, you know it's just the weather.

headlineQuote: The first time, you think it's about you. The second time, you know it's just the weather.
portrait: Tara is a fifty-eight-year-old former accounts clerk whose office job was replaced by software in 2023, after which she retrained and joined a small kitchen fitting firm as its junior. She uses AI every day for layouts and quotes and has become the firm's computer person. Calm and steady pictures suit her, since she can sit between customers and fitters. Two-year AGI makes her anxious because it follows her into the trade she chose for safety, but she'd move straight to selling and installing robots, and with five or ten years she sees a business plan rather than a threat.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would undo her move from an office into a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Short, cheap courses that start as soon as robots arrive, and help for small firms to buy them so it isn't only the giants.
